# Correlation, causation and confounding (`correlation_causation_confounding`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, controlled_trial, epidemiology_mapping
- Core idea: That two things occur together, or one after the other, does not show that one causes the other: the cause may run the other way, a third factor may produce both, or it may be chance. Fever follows swamp air, but the hidden third factor is the mosquito that breeds in the swamp; the patients of the most expensive physician die more often because he is called to the worst cases. To get from association to cause, compare groups that differ only in the suspected cause, look for a dose-response (more exposure, more effect), check that the cause comes first, and best of all intervene and see whether the effect follows. Snow's comparison of London households supplied by two water companies in 1854 is the model of a 'natural experiment' when you cannot intervene.
- Pitfalls:
  - Reducing it to the slogan 'correlation is not causation' and then dismissing all observational evidence; correlation is a clue that needs explaining
  - Forgetting reverse causation and chance, and naming only confounders
  - Post hoc reasoning in one's own favour: the patient recovered after my remedy, the comet came before the king died
  - Assuming a bigger data set removes confounding; it only makes a biased answer more precise
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic writers warn against judging remedies from single outcomes; 'post hoc' fallacy catalogued by later logicians; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's rules for drug testing require that the effect follow the drug constantly and that accidental causes be excluded; europe: 1620 Bacon's tables of presence, absence and degrees; 1739 Hume on causation as constant conjunction; 1843 Mill's methods of agreement and difference; 1855 Snow's water-company comparison; 1888 Galton defines correlation; global: 1950s–1965 – smoking and lung cancer studies; 1965 Bradford Hill's considerations for inferring causation
- Read:
  - John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic (1843)
  - Austin Bradford Hill, The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation? (1965)
  - Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie, The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect (2018)
